newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Grain cuts attacked in EU farm price marathon.
newsitem.headline: Grain cuts attacked in EU farm price marathon.

text.p: An overwhelming majority of European Union agriculture ministers fiercely opposed plans to slash aid to wealthy wheat farmers at Monday's start of marathon farm price negotiations.

EU officials said that only Britain, Sweden and Denmark backed a proposal by Farm Commissioner Franz Fishler to cut payments to cereals farmers by 1.4 billion ecus ($1.6 billion) to help fund aid for beef producers hit by the mad cow crisis.
"We are rigorously against it," German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert told reporters, adding, "We expect a majority to vote against the proposal."
Ministers criticised Fischler's attempt to link a reduction in cereals aid with the annual farm price package.
They argued that the cut should be examined as part of future farm reforms to prepare for the EU's expansion eastwards and the next round of world farm trade negotiations.

"Spain is totally opposed," Spanish Farm Minister Loyola De Palacio told Reuters, explaining that the proposed reduction constituted a major change in EU farm policy and could not be tacked onto the annual farm price package.

Ministers also quoted official estimates showing there were sufficient savings in the EU's 1997 farm budget to cover the cost of help for beef producers hit by the fall in prices due to fears of BSE, the deadly cattle disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy, infecting humans.
But British Farm Minister Jack Cunningham backed Fischler.
"I hope to see support for reductions in cereals aid," he told Reuters. "There is ample evidence that there has been over-compensation for cereals."

The Commission's agriculture directorate has estimated that cereals farmers were overpaid by 8.5 billion ecus ($9.6 billion) during the past four marketing years. A British study put the excess much higher at 14.3 billion ecus ($16.2 billion).
The payments were intended to compensate farmers for cuts in support prices agreed under 1992 farm reforms to remove grain, beef and dairy surpluses and to curb costs.
Cereals prices then soared but farmers continued to be paid for losses they never suffered.
Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates said that the Commission's estimates were based on out of date figures and that grain prices had now fallen.
But Fischler was adamant, insisting that there was a financial need to make cuts in 1998.
"Fischler is ready to discuss solutions but the problem cannot be postponed," a spokesman quoted him as saying.
The Dutch EU Presidency will now hold private talks with each country to sort out their long shopping lists of sweeteners to the farm price package, a Dutch spokesman said.
The bilateral talks will continue on Tuesday and will be followed in the afternoon by a Presidency compromise, the spokesman added. Agreement is not expected until Wednesday.
